lesson.title: Kicking a piece that is already trading gains no tempo
summary: When enemy and own pieces attack each other, a pawn 'kick' gains no tempo: the enemy piece simply captures first, on its own terms.
Compare both trades: whoever captures decides the recapture. Pick the version that damages their structure, not yours (e.g. exd4 for them vs exf5 for you).
In closed centres, your centre pawn recapturing sideways often dissolves your chain and hands the opponent a permanent outpost.

lesson.title: In rook endings, don't make your rook a passive guard of a weak pawn
summary: When a weak pawn is attacked in a rook ending, compare passive defence with giving it up so your rook reaches the 7th rank or enemy pawns.
A rook tied to an isolated pawn gets hit by pawn breaks (…c5, …b5). The pawn usually falls later anyway, and your rook stays passive.
Before defending, ask whether the pawn can hold for long. If not, spend the tempo on rook activity now.

lesson.title: Queenless and worse: centralise the king, don't liquidate
summary: Once queens are off, treat the position as an endgame: bring the king to the centre before making pawn breaks.
When worse structurally or a pawn down, avoid trades that leave a pure rook ending with isolated pawns.
Score recaptures as recaptures; seeing a trade as a 'win' inflated my evaluation for the whole stretch.
lesson.why_general: In any queenless position where you are structurally worse, king activity keeps drawing chances alive, while liquidating pawn breaks hand the opponent a technically winning ending.
lesson.narrative: The slide began with 14.c3?, which kicked a knight that was already trading on f5. After 14...Nxf5 15.exf5 White was left with doubled, isolated f-pawns, a weak d3 and a pawn deficit. I misread 15.exf5 as winning a piece (+320) when it only recaptured. From then on the queenless position was really an endgame. The engine kept asking for Kf3-e4 to centralise the king, but I made middlegame moves instead: Rd1, Be3 and above all 18.d4?, which liquidated minor pieces and rooks. That left an isolated d-pawn and a passive rook in a rook ending a pawn down. Each trade I scored as 'simplifying' or 'winning a rook' was really just a recapture that turned Black's structural edge into a clean technical endgame.
lesson.misconception: I believed that opening lines and trading pieces would relieve my weak pawns, when trades only made Black's extra pawn and better structure decisive, and the real resource was king activity.

lesson.title: Don't move the last kingside defender when an enemy rook already sits on the open file
summary: Your king is castled, its rook-pawn is gone and an enemy rook is on that file: treat your kingside knight as a defender, not a target to cash in.
Before a 'saving' capture with that knight, list every queen move onto the open file (Qh4/Qh2-type). Look for mate on h1/h2 first.
If the knight is attacked, give it up (d3, then Qxf3) rather than move it away. Material is secondary to keeping the file covered.
lesson.diagnosis: Nxe5 removed the knight that covered h2 and h4. That let ...Qh4 bring the queen alongside the h8 rook on the open h-file, with an unstoppable mate on h1.
lesson.why_general: Whenever an opponent has opened a file toward your castled king, moving away the minor piece guarding the entry squares invites a queen-and-rook mate, however attractive the capture looks.

evidence: Position: `r2qkbnr/1pp2pp1/p1p5/4p3/4P1p1/5N2/PPPP1PP1/RNBQ1RK1 w kq - 0 8` — played **Nxe5**, lost 852 cp.

Refutation: 8...Qh4 9. f4 g3 10. Qh5 Qxh5 11. d4 Qh1#
Diagnosis: Nxe5 removed the knight that covered h2 and h4. That let ...Qh4 bring the queen alongside the h8 rook on the open h-file, with an unstoppable mate on h1.

lesson.title: Before a quiet rook move, check where the enemy third-rank rook can swing sideways
summary: When an enemy rook sits on its third rank, list every sideways move it has (Rh3, Rg3) that hits your loose or isolated pawns near your king.
An undefended h-pawn or g-pawn in front of a thin king shelter is a target. Defend it or create a counter-threat before making slow doubling moves.
Prefer an active unpin that gains a tempo or counterplay (attack a pawn, hit a loose piece) over keeping the outpost knight with a passive rook move.
lesson.diagnosis: I played Re7 to keep the pinned outpost knight and double rooks, but missed that White's Re3 could simply swing to h3 and win the undefended isolated h6-pawn.
lesson.why_general: Rook lifts along the third rank onto loose pawns in front of the king come up in many middlegames, and slow consolidating moves often ignore them.

lesson.title: Up a piece with the king uncastled: give material back to castle rather than knot up
summary: When the enemy queen forks several loose units, list every target, including the pawn shielding your uncastled king and rook.
If saving all the pieces leaves the king in the centre facing an open e-file, prefer returning material to castle and develop.
Before choosing a 'keeps everything' move, check what it allows: queen captures near the king, Re1+ pins, and a stuck rook.
lesson.diagnosis: I protected both knights with Ncd6 but allowed Qxg7. After that my king stayed stuck in the centre with the e-file open, Re1+ pinned a knight and my h-rook was dead, so the extra piece was worth nothing.
lesson.why_general: In gambit-style positions you are often a piece up with the king uncastled. Hanging onto all the material instead of returning some to castle is a recurring way to lose the advantage.

evidence: Position: `r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/3P4/2nQn3/2P2N2/P4PPP/R1B2RK1 b kq - 1 11` — played **Ncd6**, lost 103 cp.

Refutation: 12. Qxg7 Qf6 13. Qxf6 Nxf6 14. Re1+ Nfe4 15. Nd2 f5

Diagnosis: I protected both knights with Ncd6 but allowed Qxg7. After that my king stayed stuck in the centre with the e-file open, Re1+ pinned a knight and my h-rook was dead, so the extra piece was worth nothing.
Why general: In gambit-style positions you are often a piece up with the king uncastled. Hanging onto all the material instead of returning some to castle is a recurring way to lose the advantage.

lesson.title: When you're down material, a mate threat that lets the enemy queen trade is a blunder
summary: Before playing a queen-battery mate threat, ask: can the enemy queen simply capture mine? If yes, the threat is fake.
Down material, your compensation lives in the queens. Never put your queen where the enemy queen attacks it, unless recapturing wins something.
Prefer moves that hit the enemy queen with tempo (rook kicks) and keep the queens on while pawns storm.
lesson.diagnosis: I played Qe4 to threaten Qh7#, but e4 was attacked by Black's queen on e3, so ...Qxe4 Bxe4 traded queens and left me an exchange down in a hopeless endgame.
lesson.why_general: Battery threats often place the queen on a square the opponent's queen covers, and a material-down attacker must check for this queen trade on every attacking move.

evidence: Position: `2r2rk1/1p3pp1/p2p4/3Pp1b1/6P1/1N1Bq3/PPP4P/1K3R1Q w - - 3 23` — played **Qe4**, lost 296 cp.

Refutation: 23...Qxe4 24. Bxe4 Rc4 25. Re1 g6 26. Na5 Rc7 27. Rf1
Diagnosis: I played Qe4 to threaten Qh7#, but e4 was attacked by Black's queen on e3, so ...Qxe4 Bxe4 traded queens and left me an exchange down in a hopeless endgame.
Why general: Battery threats often place the queen on a square the opponent's queen covers, and a material-down attacker must check for this queen trade on every attacking move.

lesson.title: A pawn recapture can give away the square it was guarding
summary: Before recapturing with a pawn, list the squares it currently guards. Check which enemy piece could land on each one after the pawn leaves, and whether it arrives with tempo.
In locked centres, the square in front of the enemy pawn chain is critical. A knight landing there with tempo on your queen can force trades that kill your attack.
When kings are on opposite wings, don't win a pawn if it lets the opponent force a queen trade. Prefer a prophylactic move and keep the guard pawn.
lesson.diagnosis: I recaptured fxg4 without noticing that the f3 pawn was the only guard of e4, so ...Ne4 hit my queen and forced a queen trade that left me worse.
lesson.why_general: Pawn captures that open a file often give up control of a central outpost, and checking 'what did this pawn guard?' catches this in any structure.

evidence: Position: `2r2rk1/1p2bpp1/pq1p1n2/3Pp3/6p1/1N3P2/PPPQB2P/1K1R3R w - - 0 17` — played **fxg4**, lost 139 cp.

Refutation: 17...Ne4 18. Qa5 Qxa5 19. Nxa5 Rc7 20. Rhf1 Bg5 21. Nb3
Diagnosis: I recaptured fxg4 without noticing that the f3 pawn was the only guard of e4, so ...Ne4 hit my queen and forced a queen trade that left me worse.
Why general: Pawn captures that open a file often give up control of a central outpost, and checking 'what did this pawn guard?' catches this in any structure.

lesson.title: Before a pawn recapture, check which squares that pawn stops guarding
summary: When recapturing with a pawn in a pawn storm, list the squares it currently guards; giving them up can hand enemy knights a central outpost.
A tempo-gaining knight jump into the hole that lands on a fork matters more than a half-open file toward their king.
If pieces can recapture instead, keep the guarding pawn and open the file with a piece.
lesson.why_general: Many wing pawn breaks force a choice of recapture, and the pawn that recaptures often leaves behind holes the opponent's pieces can use for counterplay.
lesson.narrative: In a closed Najdorf structure with castling on opposite sides, I played the thematic 16.g4 to open lines against h5. That was already a little loose. The real slide came with 17.fxg4. Recapturing with the f-pawn gave up White's only guard of e4, so Black's knight jumped to e4 with tempo. From there it went to f2 and forked my rooks. I had judged the position as +2 for White because the g-file was 'opening', but in reality my pieces were tied up defending f2 and the d1/h1 rooks. I lost the exchange and kept underestimating Black's activity. That ended in 23.Qe4, which let a material-up opponent trade queens.
lesson.misconception: I thought the pawn recapture that opened a file toward the enemy king was automatically good, and ignored that the f-pawn was the only thing keeping the enemy knight out of e4 and f2.

lesson.title: Against queen and rook, choose the king's flight square by counting checks, not by heading
summary: When your exposed king faces enemy queen plus rook, list every queen check after each flight square. Follow each forcing line three or four checks deep.
Watch for squares beside your king that none of your pieces cover. A queen check there, plus the rook taking the back rank, often makes a mating net.
Pawns behind the king do not protect it if they cannot cover the squares in front of it. Prefer the flight square whose checks run out.
lesson.diagnosis: I moved my king toward the kingside pawns on general principle, but that let the enemy queen check from an adjacent square that none of my pieces covered, which led to a forced mate; the 'more exposed' square actually allowed the king to escape.
lesson.why_general: Choosing a king move under a queen-and-rook attack by general feel instead of concrete check sequences is a recurring error whenever kings are exposed in open positions.

lesson.title: When ahead and checked by Q+R, block with your queen to force the trade
summary: Material up and in check, with an enemy queen plus a rook on your 7th rank near your king? First look for a queen interposition that forces a trade.
Before a king step, check every enemy check and fork that follows: rook to the back rank, queen to the 7th, and hits on your loose queen.
Trading queens takes away the attacker's main piece. A simple won ending beats a king walk that leaves loose pieces to be forked.
lesson.diagnosis: I saw that Qf6 forced a winning queen trade but chose a king step. That walked into Rb8+ and Qa7+, which chased my king and forked my loose queen.
lesson.why_general: Converting extra material against an enemy queen and active rook often fails to forcing checks. Offering the queen trade with an interposition is a common, reliable escape.

Why general: Converting extra material against an enemy queen and active rook often fails to forcing checks. Offering the queen trade with an interposition is a common, reliable escape.

lesson.title: Up a piece against checks: block with the minor piece, not the queen
summary: When a piece up and facing queen checks, interpose the knight or rook; keep your queen free to counterattack and guard pawns.
Don't force a queen trade at any price; a queen block that drops pawns or tangles your pieces gives back your edge.
Trust the material count: Q+R+N vs Q+R is winning, so play solidly rather than desperately simplifying.
lesson.why_general: Converting extra material against an exposed king with queens on comes down to blocking checks with minor pieces and keeping the queen active, whatever the structure.
lesson.narrative: Black was a clean piece up (Q+R+N vs Q+R) with the engine at +4 to +5.5 throughout, but I rated my position at only about +1 and played as if I were struggling. Against White's queen checks I kept interposing my queen (Qh4, Qc7, Qf7, Qf5) to force a queen trade. The engine wanted the knight or rook to block (Rh4, Nf7) so the queen stayed free. Blocking with the queen at move 68 let White take the a6 pawn, and each later queen block left my pieces more tangled and my king more exposed. That set up the Kf8 collapse.
lesson.misconception: I treated an immediate queen trade as the main goal, so I blocked checks with my queen, when blocking with the minor piece kept my queen active and my material safe.
